title: Assessing Temporal Consistency in Satellite‐Based and Modeled Soil Moisture Products and Its Implications for Trend Detection and Drought Monitoring
content:
Abstract

Soil moisture is a critical state variable governing land-atmosphere feedbacks, carbon cycling, and hydrological processes, yet existing long-term data sets remain constrained by limitations in temporal continuity and cross-sensor consistency. Individual remote sensing records are too short to resolve multi-decadal trends; land surface model outputs are limited by deficiencies in process representations and parameterization choices; and merged satellite records risk introducing non-physical artifacts through sensor transitions and algorithmic merging. In this study, we systematically evaluate the temporal consistency and reliability of three widely used soil moisture data sets: the European Space Agency Climate Change Initiative gap-filled merged observational product (ESA CCI), the land data assimilation-based NASA HydroGlobe, and the L-band passive microwave Soil Moisture Active Passive (SMAP) record. We assess their suitability for trend detection, uncertainty characterization, and extreme event monitoring. Our analysis reveals noticeable heterogeneity in temporal variability, signal-to-noise ratios, and probability distributions within the ESA CCI merged product that cannot be fully explained by precipitation variability. We further identify systematic regional discrepancies in seasonal soil moisture trends across all three products, persisting even in regions where internal product inconsistencies are not expected. Drought sensitivity evaluation across the Contiguous United States demonstrates that NASA HydroGlobe exhibits good skill in capturing drought anomalies, consistently outperforming the other data sets across most drought severity categories. Collectively, these findings underscore the importance of carefully accounting for product-specific assumptions, data lineage, and algorithmic choices when conducting decadal-scale hydrological and climate analyses, and highlight the need for more robust benchmarking frameworks for long-term soil moisture records.
